lesson.title: Borrowing Energy: Inside Endothermic Reactions
lesson.summary: In an endothermic reaction, the products end up with higher chemical potential energy than the reactants, so the reaction must absorb heat from its surroundings to proceed, often cooling everything nearby.
lesson.body:
An endothermic reaction is one that absorbs energy, generally as heat, from its surroundings as it proceeds. This happens because the chemical potential energy stored in the bonds of the products is higher than the potential energy stored in the bonds of the reactants. Since that extra energy has to come from somewhere, and energy cannot be created out of nothing, it is drawn in from the surroundings, which is often felt directly as a drop in temperature nearby.

The bond logic here mirrors the exothermic case exactly, just in reverse. Breaking the original reactant bonds still requires an energy input, and forming the new product bonds still releases some energy, but in an endothermic reaction the energy released by forming the products is smaller than the energy required to break the reactants apart in the first place. That leaves a net energy deficit, which the reaction has to make up by pulling additional heat in from its surroundings.

Instant cold packs used for injuries demonstrate this clearly. Inside the pack, solid ammonium nitrate dissolves into water when the inner pouch is broken, and this dissolving process pulls in enough heat from the surrounding water, and through the pack's outer wall, from the skin pressed against it, that the pack feels distinctly cold. Nothing about the process is cold in itself; it is simply removing thermal energy from its immediate surroundings faster than that energy can be replaced. Photosynthesis works the same way on a larger scale: plants absorb light energy and use it, along with carbon dioxide and water, to build higher energy sugar molecules, which is exactly why the process needs a continuous supply of sunlight to keep running and does not happen on its own in the dark.

A common misconception is worth heading off directly: absorbing energy does not mean a reaction somehow produces cold as a substance or output. It only means the reaction consumes more thermal energy from its immediate surroundings than it gives back, so it is the surroundings, not the reacting chemicals themselves, that cools down as its energy gets drawn away.
